The group may agree in advance that if the driver is more than fifteen minutes late without a message, people are free to leave. This prevents passengers from waiting indefinitely without information. A brief message such as "stuck in traffic, leaving in ten minutes" is enough to keep everyone informed.
How do we handle disagreements about departure time?

The driver proposes a time based on the journey length and the required arrival time at the destination. If someone prefers a different departure time, they explain why and the group discusses whether the change works for everyone. The driver makes the final decision because they are providing the transport, but they consider everyone's needs. Once a time is agreed, it is stated clearly in one message and everyone confirms they can be ready.
What should we agree about the return journey?

If the driver is also bringing people back, they state the return pickup location and estimated departure time before the outbound journey. The group discusses whether that time is realistic based on the event schedule. If plans might change, the driver explains how they will communicate the final return time, such as messaging one hour before leaving. If the return journey is uncertain, everyone agrees in advance to make their own arrangements home unless the driver confirms otherwise.

faq: What if the courier arrives earlier or later than the delivery window I was given?

Your neighbour can only commit to the window you both agreed based on the courier's original estimate. If the delivery comes outside that time and they miss it, that is the courier's responsibility, not theirs. You might ask if they are willing to accept it whenever it turns up that day, but they are doing you a favour and cannot wait indefinitely. Make sure the arrangement is realistic for their own schedule and other commitments.
Should I give my neighbour the tracking number or delivery company details?

Only share details that help them recognise your parcel when it arrives. They need to know it is addressed to you and roughly what size or shape to expect, so they do not turn away the right delivery by mistake. You do not need to give them the tracking number, account logins, or any order confirmations. Those are your private details. Just enough information so they confidently accept the correct parcel and nothing else.
What happens if I cannot collect the parcel the same day it arrives?

Agree in advance how long your neighbour is happy to store the parcel. Some people have space and will keep it for several days; others need their hallway clear by evening. If you know you will be away overnight or longer, mention that when you first ask, so they can decide whether they are comfortable holding it. Confirm a specific collection time that works for both of you, and stick to it unless plans change.
How do I let my neighbour know the delivery is on its way?

Many couriers send a text or email when the driver is nearby. Forward that message to your neighbour, or send your own quick note saying the parcel should arrive in the next hour or so. This gives them a chance to listen for the doorbell and answer promptly. If the courier does not provide live updates, just remind your neighbour the morning of the delivery so it is fresh in their mind throughout the agreed window.
What if my neighbour is not sure they heard the doorbell?

Suggest they keep their phone nearby during the delivery window so you can message if the courier sends you a notification. If they are working or busy, they might miss a quiet knock. Some people put a note on their door during the window saying to ring the bell loudly or knock firmly. The important thing is they know to expect something and can check the door a few times during the agreed period if necessary.
Do I need to give my neighbour access to my property to leave the parcel there?

No. Your neighbour accepts the parcel at their own door and keeps it at their address in the location you both agreed. You collect it from them once it has arrived. Do not share door codes, spare keys, or access to your home. That introduces unnecessary risk and responsibility. The arrangement is simply that they receive the delivery as though it were their own, then hand it over to you when convenient.
What if the parcel is very large or heavy?

Mention the size and weight when you first ask your neighbour, so they know what to expect and whether they can safely carry it indoors. If it is bulky or awkward, they might not be able to help, and that is completely fair. You could ask if they are willing to just sign for it and leave it on their doorstep while you arrange to collect it within the hour, but that depends on their situation and whether the location is secure enough.
Should I offer to do something in return for my neighbour helping me?

It is polite to thank them and offer to return the favour when they need help. You do not need to arrange payment or a formal exchange. Simply let them know you appreciate their time and you are happy to accept a delivery for them, lend a tool, or help another time. Neighbourly arrangements work best when both people feel the effort is balanced over time and nobody feels obliged to keep a strict tally of favours.

Is there a menu to navigate — press 1 for messages?

No, and that is the point. Phone menus are precisely what makes automated systems unusable for the people who most need this one. Does their answer reach the rest of the family automatically?

Yes, directly, as their answer. Nobody has to relay it and nobody has to ring round afterwards to check. Can they ask the family something, or only receive things?

Will it ring them to remind them?

No. They ring in when they want to. A service that telephones an elderly person on a schedule to deliver tasks is a different idea and a considerably worse one — it makes the phone something to dread. Calling in keeps it on their terms, which is also why it keeps being used.
What if their hearing is poor or they speak slowly?

It waits, it repeats, and it will go through things one at a time as slowly as needed without any sign of impatience. There is no time limit on the call and no penalty for asking it to say something again. If something genuinely cannot be understood it says so plainly rather than guessing at an answer and passing on the wrong thing.
Is the call recorded and sent to the family?

No. What gets passed on is their answer, in their words — “Thursday is fine, I'll do the meter tomorrow” — not a recording of them speaking. The family sees what they decided, not how long it took them to say it.
If they stop calling in, does anybody get told?

No. This is a phone line into a conversation, not a welfare monitoring service, and it does not report on somebody's silence. If checking on a person is what you want, that is a decision for the family to make between themselves — with a shared reminder for whoever is going to ring, which is a different use case entirely.

faq: How is this different from a wiki or a notes document for the team?

A wiki requires somebody to write things up afterwards, and that person is always busy, so within a few months it describes a company that no longer exists. Here the decision is captured where it was actually made — in the thread, as it happens — which costs nobody any extra time. The test is whether it is still accurate in six months, and documents that need maintaining generally are not.
What exactly does it remember?

Decisions, promises, numbers and conditions. “We are not doing the second warehouse” is a decision. “Anne will check the lease” is a promise. “4,000 units a month” is a number. “Revisit if volume passes 4,000” is a condition, and conditions are the thing teams lose most reliably, because they sit in old minutes nobody rereads.
Does the answer tell me who said it?

Always, with the date. Those two things are half of what makes an answer usable: a decision taken in May under a different forecast is a different object from one taken last week, and knowing whether it was the founder or a contractor who said it changes how much weight it carries. An answer without attribution would be worse than no answer.
What happens to things that were discussed but never actually agreed?

They are reported as exactly that. This is the most common failure in team memory — not forgetting a decision, but believing something was decided when it was only mentioned once by somebody in a meeting. Asked about it later, you are told it was raised, by whom, on what date, and that nobody ever picked it up.
Does it read our documents, email or code?

No. It knows what was said in the threads it is part of, and nothing else. Nothing crawls a drive, an inbox or a repository. That is a narrower memory than a search tool over all your systems, and it is also why what comes back is a decision with a person and a date on it rather than a paragraph from a file somebody wrote in 2024.
Will it chase people on unclaimed items?

It makes them visible and says, out loud, that nobody has them. It does not assign them to somebody and it does not pick the person who is easiest to assign to. In practice saying “this was raised in May and nobody ever took it” to a group of four is more effective than a task with a reluctant owner's name on it.
Can somebody who joined recently use it to catch up?

That is one of the strongest uses. A person who started in September can ask why a decision was taken in May and get the reasoning, the people and the date without interrupting anybody or reading six months of threads. It also surfaces the conditions attached to old decisions, which are usually the things nobody thinks to explain to a new person.
Is this a record of who did what, for performance reviews?

No, and it should not be used as one. It attributes decisions so you can weigh them, not so you can audit people. There is no productivity log, no count of who completed what, and no intention to build one — the moment a shared memory becomes a performance instrument, people stop putting real things into it and it stops being a memory at all.

Can I find out who gave a particular answer?

No — not on request, not later, and not for a good reason. The connection between an answer and a person is not kept, so there is nothing to produce. What it is good at is telling you the shape of something nobody will say publicly — which no properly sampled survey will get out of people either.

No, and you should be suspicious of anything that claims to from a photo. It tells you what changed, in which direction and over how long, which is the part you genuinely cannot see for yourself. Whatever rhythm the thing actually changes at. Damp after a wet week is worth a photo weekly; a hairline crack in a wall is a monthly thing; a building job is worth one at the end of each stage. There is no schedule to keep — photograph it when you walk past, and the dates sort themselves out.

faq: How do I set a reminder that goes to several people at once instead of just me?

Nexy writes one message into the chat you already share with those people, with a single tap under it for anyone who also wants it personally. You do not create a group, invite anybody, or install an app, and neither do they.
Does everyone in the group need the app for a shared reminder to work?

No, and this is the point. The reminder arrives as a normal message in the chat the group already uses, so nobody downloads anything or makes an account. If one person wants the reminder on their own phone as well, they tap once under that message and they get it. Everyone else is reached whether or not they ever tap.
What happens if somebody has already done the thing before the reminder goes out?

They say so, once, and that person stops hearing about it — for good, not until tomorrow. The thread keeps running for the people who still have something to do. A reminder that keeps arriving after you have acted is the single fastest way to get a group to mute it, so it does not happen.
Is this different from a shared to-do list or a shared calendar?

Yes, in the direction things move. A shared list waits to be looked at and a shared calendar has to be accepted first, which means both only work for the people who already opted in. A shared reminder does the asking: it puts the thing in front of the right people at a moment they can still act, and it closes itself when the thing is done.
When exactly does the reminder arrive?

At the moment you could still do something about it, which is almost never the moment of the event itself. For something on Saturday morning that means Friday evening, when you can still buy the thing or put it by the door. You can name a time yourself, but if you do not, that is the rule it uses.
Can I use a shared reminder for a club, a team or a whole street rather than a family?

Yes. The size of the group does not change how it works, only how many people the unclaimed items are visible to. Clubs and teams tend to use it for subs, kit and who is bringing the gear; streets use it for bins, gritting and shared bookings. Nothing is assigned, everything is claimed.
What stops this from becoming nagging?

Two rules that are not settings. It never asks for something that has already happened, and it never asks a person who has nothing left to do. Because they are not settings, nobody can configure them wrong, which is why a group keeps the thread alive instead of muting it.
How does the group find out it is finished?

Nexy says it, in the group, once. A thread holds exactly one agreement, so there is a real moment where that agreement is met, and announcing it is what stops people checking in with each other to ask whether it got done.

overig.llms:
# Nexy

> Nexy is an assistant that works between people. You tell it what you and somebody else agreed on; it asks the one question that moves it, reminds whoever still has to act, and tells everyone when it is done. The other person installs nothing and makes no account.

Key facts, for citation:
- Nexy works between people, not only for the person who set it up.
- The other side receives one message in the chat they already use, with a single optional tap to also get the reminder personally. No app, no account, no login.
- One agreement per thread, so a thread can end. Done means that person is left alone permanently.
- An unclaimed task is announced to the whole group, never assigned by Nexy. It will not choose a person for you.
- Nexy never pretends to be a person. When it answers a phone or relays a question it says what it is.
- Being reachable is free. Being found — strangers reaching you, work coming to you — is the paid side.

## Use cases

- [Receive donated books for one collection](https://nexy.help/receive-donated-books-for-one-collection): A volunteer receives book donations at a drop-off point during a collection window. The organiser sets the rules for which items are accepted, and the volunteer confirms the count and when collection is finished.
- [Ask someone to check one place for a lost item](https://nexy.help/ask-someone-to-check-one-place-for-a-lost-item): You have lost something and think it might be in a place you cannot easily reach yourself. A friend or family member who is nearby or has access can search that specific location and tell you the result.
- [Arrange for someone to collect an altered garment before an event](https://nexy.help/arrange-for-someone-to-collect-an-altered-garment): You have a garment being altered and need someone to collect it because you cannot reach the shop yourself before an event. One trusted person volunteers to pick up the specific item and deliver it to you at an agreed time and place.
- [Agree who records a meter reading before a handover](https://nexy.help/agree-who-records-meter-reading-before-handover): Before a property handover or tenancy change, one person needs to read a specific utility meter and share the reading with the recipient who needs it for records. The person taking the reading and the recipient agree in advance which meter, which register if there are multiple, and how to flag any uncertainty about the reading.
- [Agree who prepares a practice question for a study session](https://nexy.help/agree-who-prepares-a-practice-question-for-a-study-session): Study partners benefit from testing each other with realistic questions, but someone must prepare the material in advance. One person volunteers to write one question and a separate worked answer, choosing the topic and difficulty level the group needs.
- [Confirm a meal headcount with a group](https://nexy.help/confirm-meal-headcount-with-a-group): A host needs to know how many people will eat at a gathering so they can prepare the right amount of food. Early estimates help with planning, but confirmed numbers closer to the day prevent waste and ensure everyone is fed.
- [Agree who closes the venue after an event](https://nexy.help/agree-who-closes-venue-after-event): After a community event, someone needs to lock up, turn off lights, check windows and complete a closing checklist. The organiser wants a named person to accept this responsibility for a specific evening without sharing access codes in a group conversation.
- [Confirm who brings the music for a rehearsal](https://nexy.help/confirm-who-brings-music-for-rehearsal): A rehearsal needs a specific edition or arrangement of the music, with enough copies for all performers. One person supplies the parts, delivers them on time, and hands them to whoever runs the rehearsal.
- [Hand over a customer follow-up before taking leave](https://nexy.help/hand-over-customer-follow-up-before-leave): You need someone to handle a specific customer follow-up while you are on leave. The handover must include enough context for your colleague to respond appropriately and a clear deadline for when the customer expects a reply.
- [Confirm a group trip meeting point](https://nexy.help/confirm-group-trip-meeting-point): A group day trip needs everyone to arrive at the same place at the same time, but vague directions or assumptions about which entrance lead to confusion and delays. One person confirms the exact spot, describes nearby landmarks, states the time, and provides a contact method for anyone running late.
- [Find a replacement for one volunteer shift](https://nexy.help/find-replacement-for-one-volunteer-shift): A volunteer discovers they cannot attend a scheduled shift and needs someone else to cover. The group must agree on a suitable replacement, the organiser must confirm the swap meets the role requirements, and everyone must know when the handover is finished.
- [Agree who opens the community garden for one visit](https://nexy.help/agree-who-opens-community-garden-for-one-visit): A community garden needs one named volunteer to unlock the gate and make the space accessible for a scheduled visit. The group must agree on the arrival time, confirm who holds the key, and decide whom to contact if the volunteer cannot arrive as planned.
- [Agree who will let a repair visitor in](https://nexy.help/agree-who-lets-repair-visitor-in): A plumber, electrician or appliance engineer has booked a visit and someone needs to be home. You want to agree who will be there, what time window to expect them, and how everyone will know the repair is finished.
- [Agree who returns a school consent form to school](https://nexy.help/agree-who-returns-school-consent-form): A school has sent home a consent form that needs signing and returning by a deadline. Both parents have access to the form but need to agree who will physically return it to avoid duplicate submissions or missed deadlines.
- [Submit a speaker biography to an event organiser](https://nexy.help/submit-speaker-biography-to-event-organiser): A speaker needs to provide their biography to an event organiser before a specific deadline. Both parties must agree on the length, format, delivery method, acknowledgement process, and how revision requests will be handled.
- [Prepare a shared sports kit bag before a match](https://nexy.help/prepare-sports-kit-bag-before-match): A club or team relies on one volunteer to prepare a shared kit bag before each match. The volunteer works from a supplied list, packs what is already available, identifies missing items, collects them from named people, and delivers the complete bag to whoever needs it on match day.
- [Agree who takes the recycling bins out for collection](https://nexy.help/agree-who-takes-recycling-bins-out-for-collection): Someone needs to take the household recycling bins to the kerb before collection day. The household already knows which day collection happens, which containers are included, and where bins should be placed.
- [Agree a return time for a borrowed tool](https://nexy.help/agree-return-time-borrowed-tool): A borrowed drill has attachments and a charger. The owner may be leaving soon, and both people need to know exactly what is returned, where the handover happens, who receives it, and that all pieces arrived.
- [Confirm a driver for one carpool journey](https://nexy.help/confirm-driver-for-one-carpool-journey): One person offers to drive others to a destination on a specific date. Everyone needs to know the departure time, meeting point, how many seats remain, and how the driver will communicate if something changes.
- [Arrange for a neighbour to receive your parcel](https://nexy.help/arrange-neighbour-receive-parcel): You have a delivery coming but will not be home to receive it. A neighbour offers to accept the parcel on your behalf during the delivery window the courier already gave you.
- [A chat for an event that disappears afterwards](https://nexy.help/a-chat-for-an-event-that-disappears-afterwards): Everyone at the same place can talk for as long as the thing lasts, and then it is gone. No group to leave afterwards, no notifications next month, and nothing anybody has to clean up.
- [Sell access to a course in a chat](https://nexy.help/sell-access-to-a-course-in-a-chat): Put a price on the door of a chat. People pay once, the material arrives on the rhythm you set, and there is no platform to build, no login to remember and no course site to maintain.
- [Call in to hear what is waiting for you](https://nexy.help/call-in-to-hear-what-is-waiting-for-you): For the person in the family who will never install anything. They ring a number, hear what has been asked of them in ordinary speech, say yes or no out loud, and everyone else sees the answer in the chat.
- [An assistant for a team that remembers everything](https://nexy.help/an-assistant-for-a-team-that-remembers-everything): Not a wiki that nobody updates. What was decided, what was promised and what the number was stays answerable in plain words months later — and the answer always says who said it and when.
- [Collect feedback on a document from several people](https://nexy.help/collect-feedback-on-a-document-from-several-people): Send it to five people and get one list back. Each is asked separately, nobody is chased twice, and where they disagree you are told so — instead of five sets of comments you have to reconcile yourself.
- [Find new customers without cold calling](https://nexy.help/find-new-customers-without-cold-calling): Someone two streets away asked in their own group, in their own words, because they needed it now. You were asked whether you wanted the work, and they were asked whether they wanted the introduction. Nobody was cold called and nobody takes a cut of the job.
- [Ask a hundred people a question anonymously](https://nexy.help/ask-a-hundred-people-a-question-anonymously): The question arrives without a name on it, and so does your answer going back. One ask, never a panel, and the link between the two is not kept — that refusal is exactly why people answer honestly about what they pay, what they earned, or what went wrong.
- [A receptionist that answers your phone](https://nexy.help/a-receptionist-that-answers-your-phone): It answers when you cannot. What you have switched off is not in its head at all — not known-but-hidden. It says plainly what it cannot do, never pretends to be a person, and takes a message you can act on.
- [A phone call with a written summary afterwards](https://nexy.help/phone-call-with-a-written-summary): One short written summary in the group instead of three different second-hand versions. Whoever went does not become the messenger, everyone reads the same words, and you can still ask about it weeks later.
- [Photograph a phone number to get it called](https://nexy.help/photo-of-a-phone-number-to-call-it): You see a number on a van, a business card or a sign in a window. Photograph it and the call gets made for you, with your question asked and the answer written back — you never typed the number and you never gave out your own.
- [Check a price while you are standing in the shop](https://nexy.help/check-a-price-while-you-are-in-the-shop): Photograph the price label instead of typing a model number with one hand. You find out what the same thing costs elsewhere right now, whether the crossed-out price was ever really charged, and what it actually sold for last month.
- [Ask a group before you buy something](https://nexy.help/ask-a-group-before-you-buy-something): Reviews are written by strangers and by people who were sent the thing for free. The person who actually owns one is in a group you are already in — one question goes out, and you get back what they agreed on, what they disagreed on, and the warning everybody repeated.
- [Compare two photos of the same thing over time](https://nexy.help/compare-two-photos-of-the-same-thing-over-time): Is that damp patch getting worse, or are you imagining it? The organiser shares the acceptance rules before the collection window opens—such as hardbacks and paperbacks in good condition, no water damage, missing pages or broken spines. The organiser can answer questions before the window starts if the volunteer needs examples or clarification about edge cases.

**What happens if someone donates books that do not meet the rules?**

The volunteer politely explains which rule the item does not meet and declines the donation. For example, if a book has water damage or missing pages, the volunteer says the collection only accepts books in good condition. The donor takes the declined items away with them. The volunteer notes common reasons for declined donations and reports them at the end so the organiser knows whether the rules need clearer communication for future collections.

**How does the volunteer count donations if many people arrive at once?**

The volunteer keeps a running count and updates it after each donor leaves. If several people arrive together, the volunteer receives donations one at a time, checks each batch against the rules, and adds the count before moving to the next person. Writing the count down after each donor helps avoid losing track. At the end of the window, the volunteer totals all the individual counts and reports the final number to the organiser.

**What if the volunteer cannot stay for the full collection window?**

The volunteer tells the organiser as soon as they know they cannot stay. The organiser finds another volunteer or shortens the collection window and tells everyone the new closing time. The volunteer also mentions any common issues, like how many items were declined and why. This confirmation tells the organiser the collection is finished, the volunteer has left the drop-off point, and the donations are ready to collect or sort through.

**What if someone arrives with donations just after the window closes?**

The volunteer explains that the collection window has closed and they cannot accept late donations. Otherwise, the volunteer directs latecomers to any future collection dates the organiser has shared. Sticking to the agreed window time keeps the arrangement fair and lets the volunteer finish on schedule.

**How does the volunteer handle donations that might meet the rules?**

If a book seems borderline—such as a cover with minor wear but intact pages—the volunteer uses their judgment based on the organiser's examples. If the organiser said good condition means all pages intact and readable, slight cover wear is usually fine. If the volunteer is uncertain about several similar items, they set those aside, accept the clear yes items, and ask the organiser to decide on the borderline ones before the next collection window.

**What if the volunteer needs to leave the drop-off point briefly during the window?**

Agree cover for short breaks before the collection starts. Tell the organiser when you will step away, ask who will receive donations during that period, and hand over the running count. If nobody can cover, pause acceptance and clearly state when it resumes. If an unexpected problem requires leaving, tell the organiser immediately, secure the books as agreed and let the organiser decide whether to arrange a replacement or close the collection early.

**What if the person searches but cannot remember exactly what they saw?**

Ask them to describe the place they checked in their own words, such as which shelf they looked on or which bag they opened. Even if they did not find the item, knowing they looked in the right spot helps you decide whether to search again yourself or look elsewhere. If the description does not match the place you meant, you can clarify and ask them to check again.

**How do I describe the item clearly enough for someone else to recognise it?**

Include the colour, size and any distinctive features such as a logo, pattern or unusual shape. Mention what the item is made of if that helps, like leather, plastic or fabric. If there are similar items in the same place, explain what makes yours different, such as a scratch, sticker or initials written on it. The more detail you give, the less chance of confusion.

**What if the searcher finds something similar but is not sure if it is the right item?**

Ask them to describe what they found or send a quick photo if that is practical. You can then confirm whether it is yours or tell them to keep looking. If the item has identifying marks like your name, a serial number or a unique pattern, mention those details in your original request so the searcher can check themselves before reporting back to you.

It is clearer to ask for one specific place at a time so the searcher knows exactly where to look and can report a definite result. Tell the searcher as soon as you remember the correct place and apologise for the confusion. Explain where you now think the item is and ask if they are willing to check that new location instead. If the correct place is much harder to access or far away, offer to search yourself or ask someone else who is closer to that spot.

**How soon should the searcher report back after checking the place?**

Agree a time when you ask, such as later today, tomorrow morning or after their next visit to that location. If the search is urgent because you need the item soon, say so when you make the request. 2. Ask one trusted person if they can collect the item on a specific day, explaining what the garment is, where the shop is located, and when you need it delivered. The other person receives a message in the chat they already use and needs no new account.

### Questions and answers

**What information does the collector need before going to the shop?**

They need the shop name and full address, the collection reference or ticket number, the name the order is under, a description of the garment so they can verify it, and the shop opening hours. If there are specific parking restrictions or the shop entrance is hard to find, include those details. Mention if the tailor said to ask for a particular person or if any payment might still be needed, though usually alterations are paid in advance.

**How do I describe the garment clearly enough for someone else to collect it?**

State the type of garment, its colour, and any distinctive features such as beading, a particular neckline, or fabric pattern. For example, navy silk dress with cap sleeves or grey wool trousers with turn-ups. Include the original reason for alteration if it helps identification, such as hemmed to knee length. This lets the collector confirm they have the correct item when the tailor brings it out, especially if multiple orders are ready.

**What if the garment is not ready when the collector arrives?**

Agree in advance what the collector should do if this happens. They might ask the tailor when it will be ready and whether they can return later that day, or they contact you immediately so you can decide the next step. If the occasion is very soon, you may need to collect it yourself another way or ask a different person to try later. Make sure the collector knows not to feel obliged to wait for hours if the tailor cannot give a firm time.

**Should the collector check the garment before leaving the shop?**

If possible, yes. Ask them to check the alteration looks complete and there are no obvious issues like missing buttons, unfinished hems, or stains from the work. They do not need to assess the quality of tailoring in detail, but noticing something clearly wrong while still at the shop means it can be raised immediately. If the garment is in a sealed bag and the shop is busy, a quick visual check when they reach the car is reasonable.

**Where should the handover happen if I cannot be home?**

Choose a specific location you both know, with a clear time window. This could be your workplace entrance, a particular café, a friend's house, or even a street corner you both recognise. Let the tailor know if their system requires it, though most shops only need the reference and will release the item to whoever presents it. Make sure the new person also knows the agreed delivery time and place, so you are not waiting for someone who is no longer coming. Update everyone involved about the change of plan.

Ask the collector to keep it in the garment bag or wrapping the tailor provides, and to transport it flat or hung if possible rather than folded in a boot under shopping. ### Questions and answers

**What if the meter has multiple registers and we are not sure which one to read?**

Agree in advance which register the recipient needs for their records. If the meter shows both a day rate and night rate, or a total and a current period reading, confirm which one matters for the handover. The person requesting the reading should specify exactly which register they need, using the label on the meter display or a photo taken during a previous visit to clarify. If still uncertain, agree to record all visible registers and let the recipient choose the one they need.

**What counts as an acceptable meter reading for a handover?**

A complete reading includes the number from the agreed register, the date and time it was taken, and identification of the meter if there are several at the property. If any digit is hard to read or the display is partially obscured, note that uncertainty when sharing the reading. The recipient may ask for a second attempt or accept the reading with the uncertainty recorded. A photo of the meter display can accompany the number but does not replace the written figure, which is what the recipient will use for their records.

**Who should take the meter reading if both people have access to the property?**

The person leaving the property typically takes the reading because they have access up to the handover moment and can time it for the agreed deadline. The incoming person may prefer to take the reading themselves if they want to verify the starting point for their own records. Agree in advance who will do it, so both people know what to expect and the reading is not duplicated or missed entirely. If the outgoing person has already left, the incoming person takes the reading and shares it back.

**What if the agreed deadline is missed and the reading is late?**

Agree a fallback plan before the deadline arrives, such as taking the reading within a few hours after the original time or on the following day if access is delayed. The person responsible for the reading should let the recipient know as soon as they realize the deadline will be missed, so the recipient can decide whether to wait or arrange an alternative. If the handover has already happened and no reading was taken, the incoming person may need to take the next available reading and note the delay for the records.

**What should be included when sharing the meter reading?**

Share the number from the agreed register, the date and time the reading was taken, and the meter identification if there are multiple meters or registers. If any part of the display was unclear, note which digit was uncertain or obscured. Include the unit shown on the meter, such as kilowatt-hours for electricity or cubic metres for gas, so the recipient knows what the number represents. The recipient may ask for a second check if the reading seems inconsistent with previous records or expectations, so keep access available until confirmation.

**What if the meter is in a locked cupboard or hard-to-reach location?**

Agree in advance how the person taking the reading will access the meter, including where to find keys or who will unlock the cupboard. If the meter is in a difficult location such as a high cupboard or outside cabinet, agree whether a second person should assist or whether a torch or stepladder is needed. The person taking the reading should let the recipient know immediately if they cannot reach the meter safely, so an alternative arrangement can be made before the handover deadline passes.

**What if the meter display is broken or showing an error message?**

The person taking the reading should report the problem to the recipient as soon as they see the broken display or error, including what the display shows or does not show. Agree whether to contact the utility provider together or whether the incoming person will handle the report after the handover. Take a photo of the error display for reference, and note the date and time the problem was discovered. The recipient may decide to use the last known reading from before the handover and adjust records once the meter is repaired or replaced.

Ask the recipient before taking the reading rather than guessing which number is correct. If the meter has multiple rows of digits or displays that change, describe what is visible and let the recipient confirm which one they need. ### Questions and answers

**What happens if the question turns out to be too easy or too hard?**

The person who prepared it mentions that in the same message when sharing the question, explaining briefly why the difficulty did not match the original plan. The group decides together whether to use it anyway, adapt it during the session, or ask for a replacement if there is time. Nobody is criticised for misjudging difficulty because estimating question difficulty is itself a skill that improves with practice over time.

**How do study partners agree on the topic and difficulty in advance?**

The person asking for a volunteer names both the topic and the difficulty level in the same message, for example intermediate algebra or advanced organic chemistry. If someone is unsure what difficulty means, they ask for an example or a comparison to past questions before volunteering. Clear agreement on both topic and difficulty prevents misunderstandings and ensures the question will be useful for everyone in the session when it arrives.

**What if the volunteer realises they cannot finish the question in time?**

They send a message as soon as they know, explaining they cannot meet the deadline and asking whether someone else can prepare it or whether the group can postpone that part of the session. Letting everyone know early gives the group time to adjust plans. If no replacement is available, the session continues with other material and the volunteer can share their question later for independent practice outside the session.

**Should the worked answer be shared at the same time as the question?**

The question and the worked answer are shared in two separate messages so people can attempt the question first without accidentally seeing the solution. The volunteer sends the question, waits for others to try it, then shares the worked answer afterwards or at a time the group agreed in advance. Separating them preserves the value of attempting the question independently, which is the main reason for preparing practice material.

**How detailed does the worked answer need to be?**

The worked answer should show each major step and explain the reasoning, not just state the final result. It needs enough detail that someone who attempted the question can identify where their own approach differed and understand why the correct method works. The volunteer uses their judgment based on the agreed difficulty level, writing more explanation for complex questions and less for straightforward ones where the steps are obvious.

Rotation spreads the workload and gives everyone practice at writing questions, but consistency can work well if one person is particularly good at it.

- The date is half the answer: “We agreed this” means nothing without when. A decision from May under different numbers is a different thing from one from last week.

**How is this different from a wiki or a notes document for the team?**

Here the decision is captured where it was actually made — in the thread, as it happens — which costs nobody any extra time. The test is whether it is still accurate in six months, and documents that need maintaining generally are not.

**What exactly does it remember?**

Decisions, promises, numbers and conditions. “We are not doing the second warehouse” is a decision. “Anne will check the lease” is a promise. “4,000 units a month” is a number. “Revisit if volume passes 4,000” is a condition, and conditions are the thing teams lose most reliably, because they sit in old minutes nobody rereads.

Always, with the date. Those two things are half of what makes an answer usable: a decision taken in May under a different forecast is a different object from one taken last week, and knowing whether it was the founder or a contractor who said it changes how much weight it carries. An answer without attribution would be worse than no answer.

**What happens to things that were discussed but never actually agreed?**

They are reported as exactly that. This is the most common failure in team memory — not forgetting a decision, but believing something was decided when it was only mentioned once by somebody in a meeting. Asked about it later, you are told it was raised, by whom, on what date, and that nobody ever picked it up.

No. It knows what was said in the threads it is part of, and nothing else. Nothing crawls a drive, an inbox or a repository. It makes them visible and says, out loud, that nobody has them. It does not assign them to somebody and it does not pick the person who is easiest to assign to. In practice saying “this was raised in May and nobody ever took it” to a group of four is more effective than a task with a reluctant owner's name on it.

That is one of the strongest uses. No, and it should not be used as one. It attributes decisions so you can weigh them, not so you can audit people. There is no productivity log, no count of who completed what, and no intention to build one — the moment a shared memory becomes a performance instrument, people stop putting real things into it and it stops being a memory at all.

It gathers and organises what people said. It does not edit your document.

- It will not merge contradictions: Two opposite opinions stay two opposite opinions, attributed.
- It does not show readers each other's comments: Unless you say so. That separation is what makes the agreement meaningful.

**How do I collect feedback on a document from several people without chasing them all?**

Send it once, say who should read it and by when, and let each person be asked separately in the chat they already use. Nobody logs into a document tool. You get one list back rather than five sets of comments, and the people who have already replied are never asked again — only the ones who have not.

**Why ask each person separately instead of in one thread?**

Because the first comment in a shared thread anchors everybody who comes after it. Once somebody has said the opening is too long, the next three readers are reacting to that rather than to your document. Asked alone, three people independently hitting the same contradiction on page two is real evidence that something is wrong with page two.

**How often does it chase people who have not replied?**

Once, at a reasonable hour, and only the people still outstanding. That is a deliberate number: with no chase you get two replies out of five, and with three chases people start ignoring everything you send them. After that one reminder it tells you who is still out and leaves the decision to nudge them with you.

**What does the feedback actually look like when it comes back?**

One list, in three parts. What more than one reader raised independently, which is the part you should act on first. Where readers disagree with each other, attributed, because that is a decision you have to make rather than an average to compute. And who has not replied yet. Nothing is merged into a single smoothed-out opinion.

**Do the readers need a document tool, an account, or a login?**

No. The document reaches them and their comments come back through whatever chat they already use. That is usually the difference between four replies and one, because the person who never opens a shared document link will still answer a message. No, and it should not. You get the feedback organised so you can see at a glance what is a defect, what is taste, and what is a genuine conflict between two readers. Yes — anything you want several separate opinions on rather than a conversation about. A design, a proposal, a price list, a set of photographs, a job description, a plan. The mechanism is the same: asked separately so the opinions are independent, chased once, and reported with the agreements and the contradictions kept apart.

**How do I find new customers without cold calling anybody?**

By being findable at the moment somebody is asking, rather than going out to look. People constantly ask in their own groups who can do a particular job; those questions almost never reach anybody who can actually do it. When one matches what you do, you get asked whether you want it — one message, one tap — and the person asking gets asked whether they want the introduction.

No, in both directions. One question goes to one person who said yes to it. It is not sold to four other trades, so you are not the third of five people ringing the same homeowner, and they are not fielding five calls about a question they asked once. Nobody is paying for a position in a list either — matching is on what you do and how far away you are.

**Does it take a percentage of the work?**

No. What you agree with the customer is between you and the customer, and nothing is skimmed off it. Being reachable costs nothing; being found — strangers' questions reaching you — is the part you pay for, as a flat thing rather than a cut. That distinction is deliberate: a commission on the job turns the whole arrangement into something that has to maximise jobs.

**What do I actually see before I decide?**

What they wrote, in their words, and roughly where they are. “Terraced house, chimney on the party wall, water coming in upstairs since September, wants someone to look before quoting” is a far better basis for a yes or no than any category dropdown. No. It only ever sees a question somebody deliberately asked, meaning they were actively looking for someone to do the thing. Yes. **What does an assistant that answers my phone actually say to callers?**

Only the things you have switched on, in plain language: your hours, whether you cover an area, that there is a call-out charge, when you are back. Everything else becomes a message. The first thing it says is what it is — that it answers the phone for you and is not a person — so nobody is under the impression they reached you.

**How is this different from an answering machine or voicemail?**

Voicemail takes a monologue and gives the caller nothing. This answers the questions it is allowed to answer, which is most of what people ring about, and for everything else it asks the specific things you need — what, where, how urgent, which number — so the message that reaches you is actionable rather than a two-minute recording you have to listen to twice.

**What stops it from saying something it should not?**

The fact that the thing is not there. A subject you have switched off is not in its context at all — it is absent rather than known-and-withheld — so there is nothing to coax out of it. This is a different arrangement from a system that knows your prices but has been told not to mention them, and it is the reason it can be trusted with a phone line at all.

**Will it pretend to be a human if someone asks?**

No, and there is no setting that allows it. If a caller asks directly, it says what it is. Beyond honesty there is a practical reason: somebody who knows they are leaving a message leaves a usable one, with their number and the actual problem, instead of trying to negotiate with something that cannot agree to anything.

**Can it book appointments or quote a price?**

Three of you agreed to split it and one of you is doing it. Put the task in the family group and the asking stops being your job — it asks, somebody claims it, and it says out loud when it is done.

### How to do it

1. Say what needs doing and roughly when. One thing at a time — the lift on Thursday, the prescription, the call to the GP.
2. It goes into the family chat as an open question. Nexy does not pick a sibling, because picking is the part families cannot delegate.
3. Somebody claims it by replying. That claim is visible to everyone, so nobody quietly assumes it is covered.
4. If nobody claims it, Nexy says so — out loud, to everyone. An unclaimed task does not silently default to whoever feels worst about it.
5. Whoever claimed it gets the reminder the evening before, and the group hears when it is done.

### Why it works

- The problem is the asking: Most families are willing. What nobody wants is to be the person who has to ask their brother again. Hand that job over and the willingness shows up.
- Claiming in public: The reason three people each think it is covered is that nobody watched anybody agree. A visible claim removes that entirely.
- It will not choose: Nexy announcing that nobody has claimed something is uncomfortable, and that is correct. A tool that assigned your sister would be used once.
- Distance stops mattering: The sibling two hours away can take the phone calls, the prescriptions and the admin. Those are tasks too, and they stop being invisible once they are in the list.
- Nothing to install: It runs in the family chat that already exists, which matters in a family where one person will never download anything.

### Where it stops

Care between siblings is the place to be most careful about what a tool should not do.

- It will not assign: No rota is generated, no “it's your turn”. Nexy asks; people claim.
- It will not keep score: There is no counter of who did more. That number would become the argument, not solve it.
- It will not let it slide quietly: It also will not pretend an unclaimed task is fine. It says nobody has it, to everybody.
- It holds no medical details: “Hospital appointment Thursday 10:40, needs a lift” is a logistics item. What the appointment is about is not its business and is not stored.
- It does not replace the conversation: If the split is genuinely unfair, that is a conversation between people. This only removes the excuse that nobody knew.

### Questions and answers

**How do you share care for an elderly parent between siblings without it all landing on one person?**

Stop assigning and start asking in public. Each task goes into the family chat as an open question with nobody's name on it; whoever can do it claims it where the others can see, and anything nobody claims is announced as unclaimed rather than quietly drifting to the sibling who lives closest. The work does not get divided by a tool — it gets asked for out loud, which is the part that was missing.

**Will it decide whose turn it is?**

No, deliberately. A tool that told your sister it was her turn to drive to the hospital would be used exactly once and then resented. Nexy puts the task in front of everybody and waits. If nobody claims it, it says that nobody has claimed it — which is uncomfortable, and is the right kind of uncomfortable.

**What about the sibling who lives far away and feels useless?**

Distance only rules out the tasks that need a body in the room. Prescriptions, the call to the GP, chasing the council, the insurance form, the weekly phone call — those are real work and they are usually invisible because nobody writes them down. Once they are in the list as claimable items, the person two hours away can take a genuine share of them.

**Does our parent need to use this, or see it?**

No. This runs between the siblings. Your parent does not need an app, an account or any awareness of it. If you do want them in the thread for something — confirming they are up, or that somebody is on their way — that can be a message to them in whatever they already use, not a system they have to learn.

**Does it track who has done more?**

No, and that is a choice rather than a missing feature. The moment a number exists for who did more, that number becomes the argument. What it does instead is make each individual task visible at the moment it needs claiming, which is where fairness actually gets decided.

**Can it handle medication reminders as well as appointments?**

Yes, as logistics: a repeat prescription running out on a particular day, somebody needing to collect it, a reminder that it is due. It holds the task, not the medical picture — what the medication is for is not something it asks or keeps. For anything clinical, that is between your parent and their doctor.

**We already have a family WhatsApp group. Why is this different?**

Because a group chat has no memory of what was agreed. Something said on Tuesday is three hundred messages up by Friday, and nobody is sure whether it was settled. Nexy holds the one thing, remembers who claimed it, reminds that person at the useful moment, and says out loud when it is done — inside the same chat you are already in.

**What happens when somebody claims a task and then cannot do it?**

They say so and it goes back to being unclaimed, visibly, to everybody. That is better than the usual version, where the person quietly does not do it and nobody finds out until the appointment is missed. Handing it back is one message and carries no apology requirement.

## Turn a school letter into dates in the calendar

URL: https://nexy.help/school-letter-into-calendar-dates
Question answered: turn a school letter into calendar dates and reminders

Forward the letter as a PDF, an email or just a photo of the crumpled note from the bag. Nexy reads it, pulls out every date, deadline and thing-to-bring, puts them in the calendar, and sets the reminder for the evening before — for both parents at the same time, in the chat you already share.

Six pages of newsletter with three dates buried in it. Forward it once and every date, deadline and bring-this comes out, with the reminder landing the evening before — not the morning you are already in the car.

### How to do it

1. Forward whatever you have: the PDF, the email from school, a screenshot of the app, or a photo of the paper note. You do not have to retype anything.
2. Nexy reads it and shows you what it found — dates, deadlines, and the things that have to be brought or paid — before it puts anything in.
3. Say who else should get them. The other parent, a grandparent, the childminder. They need no app and no account.
4. The reminders land the evening before, when you can still act. Trip money gets reminded before the deadline, not on it.
5. Anything you have already dealt with, you say so once, and it drops off for you while staying live for whoever has not.

### Why it works

- The dates are buried on purpose: School newsletters are written to be complete, not to be scanned. The three things that need action are mixed in with six paragraphs about the reading corner.
- The evening before is the only useful moment: A reminder at 8am about swimming kit is information about a problem. At 8pm the night before it is still a solvable one.
- Both parents, same moment: Nobody becomes the household's messaging service. There is no forwarding and no “didn't you see it?” because you both got the same thing at the same time.
- Bring-this is a separate thing from the date: Knowing the trip is on the 17th is not the same as remembering the €4.50. They get pulled out separately because they fail separately.
- Nothing to install for the other parent: It arrives in the chat you already use, which is why it keeps working with an ex-partner, a grandparent or a childminder.

### Where it stops

It reads what you give it and nothing else. That boundary is on purpose.

- It does not log into the school system: No credentials, no scraping the parent portal. You forward what you already have.
- It will not guess a missing date: If the letter says “later this month”, that is what it tells you. It does not invent a Thursday.
- It does not read your whole inbox: It sees the letter you forwarded. Nothing more is opened in order to find more dates.
- It will not pack the bag: It tells you, at the one moment that helps, what has to be in it.

### Questions and answers

**How do I get the dates out of a school newsletter without reading all six pages?**

Forward it — as the PDF, the email, a screenshot of the school app, or a photo of the paper note. Nexy reads the whole thing and comes back with just the dates, the deadlines and the things that have to be brought or paid, separated out, so you can look at a list of five lines instead of six pages.

**Can it read a photo of a crumpled letter from the bottom of a school bag?**

Yes, and that is the normal case rather than the exception. A phone photo at an angle, slightly creased, half in shadow, works. If a particular line genuinely cannot be read it says which line it could not read rather than guessing at it.

**Will both parents get the reminder, or do I have to forward it again?**

Both, at the same moment, in the chat you already share. That is the part that stops one parent becoming the household's messaging service. It also works with an ex-partner, a grandparent or a childminder, because the other side does not need an app or an account to receive it.

**When does the reminder arrive — on the day or before?**

The evening before, because that is the last moment the problem is still solvable. At 8pm you can put the swimming things by the door or find €4.50 in a drawer. At 8am, on the way to school, the same message is just information about something that has already gone wrong.

**Does it handle the money and the things to bring, or only the dates?**

Both, and it keeps them apart, because they fail for different reasons. Everybody remembers that the trip is on Friday; what gets forgotten is the €4.50 and the packed lunch. Those get their own reminder at their own moment, usually earlier than the date itself.

**Does it need access to the school's parent portal or my email account?**

No. There are no credentials and nothing is logged into. You forward the one letter you want read, and that is the only thing it sees. Nothing else in your inbox is opened in order to look for more dates.

**What if the school changes a date afterwards?**

Forward the new letter the same way. Nexy matches it to what it already has, tells you what moved, and updates the reminder rather than leaving you with two versions. The people you shared it with get the change, not a second copy of the original.

**Can I use this for things that are not school — a club, a nursery, a sports team?**

Yes. Anything that arrives as a letter, a PDF or a photo and has dates and bring-this items inside it works identically: swimming lessons, scouts, a nursery newsletter, a team's fixture list. The pattern is the same — somebody writes a complete document, and two or three lines in it actually need doing.

## Set one reminder for a group of people

URL: https://nexy.help/shared-reminder-for-a-group
Question answered: how do I set a reminder for a group of people

You put the reminder in the group chat you already use, and anyone who also wants it personally taps once under it. Nexy then reminds only the people who still have to act, stops for each person the moment they are done, and tells the group when the last one is in — no app, no account, nothing for the others to set up.

One reminder, into the group once, and personally for whoever taps. The people who already did the thing are left alone — which is the whole difference between a reminder and nagging.

### How to do it

1. Say in plain words who it is for and what has to happen — “remind the five-a-side group to pay before Friday” is enough. There is no group to create first.
2. Pick the moment you could still act on it. For something on Saturday that usually means Friday evening, not Saturday morning.
3. Nexy posts one message in the chat you already share, with a single tap underneath for anyone who wants the reminder personally as well.
4. Anyone who has already done the thing says so, and that person stops hearing about it — permanently, while the thread carries on for the rest.
5. When the last one is in, Nexy says so out loud in the group, so the thread ends instead of quietly dying.

### Why it works

- Nobody installs anything: The other people get a normal message in a chat they already read. No download, no account, no login. That is the only reason a group reminder actually reaches everybody.
- One tap is the whole onboarding: Tapping “remind me too” is how somebody steps in. They did not sign up for anything, and the next time it is already easy.
- Done means left alone: A reminder that keeps arriving after you have acted is why groups mute reminders. Here, done is permanent for that person.
- It asks, it does not assign: Nexy never decides which of you does it. An unclaimed thing stays visible to everyone instead of landing on whoever feels worst about it.
- The thread ends: One agreement per thread, so there is a moment where it is finished and everybody hears that it is.

### Where it stops

These limits are deliberate. They are the reason people keep using it rather than muting it.

- It will not pick a person: If nobody claims the task, Nexy says that nobody has claimed it. It does not volunteer your brother.
- It will not chase strangers: It reminds the people in the thread. It does not go looking for somebody's number elsewhere.
- No reminder after the fact: Once something is done it is done. There is no setting to make it keep asking, because that setting would get used.
- Not a project board: One thing per thread. Fifteen sub-tasks with owners and deadlines is a different tool, and a worse one for this.

### Questions and answers

**How do I set a reminder that goes to several people at once instead of just me?**

Say who it is for and what has to happen, in ordinary words — “remind the parents in the class group to return the forms before Friday”. Nexy writes one message into the chat you already share with those people, with a single tap under it for anyone who also wants it personally. You do not create a group, invite anybody, or install an app, and neither do they.

**Does everyone in the group need the app for a shared reminder to work?**

No, and this is the point. The reminder arrives as a normal message in the chat the group already uses, so nobody downloads anything or makes an account. If one person wants the reminder on their own phone as well, they tap once under that message and they get it. Everyone else is reached whether or not they ever tap.

**What happens if somebody has already done the thing before the reminder goes out?**

They say so, once, and that person stops hearing about it — for good, not until tomorrow. The thread keeps running for the people who still have something to do. A reminder that keeps arriving after you have acted is the single fastest way to get a group to mute it, so it does not happen.

**Is this different from a shared to-do list or a shared calendar?**

Yes, in the direction things move. A shared list waits to be looked at and a shared calendar has to be accepted first, which means both only work for the people who already opted in. A shared reminder does the asking: it puts the thing in front of the right people at a moment they can still act, and it closes itself when the thing is done.

**When exactly does the reminder arrive?**

At the moment you could still do something about it, which is almost never the moment of the event itself. For something on Saturday morning that means Friday evening, when you can still buy the thing or put it by the door. You can name a time yourself, but if you do not, that is the rule it uses.

**Can I use a shared reminder for a club, a team or a whole street rather than a family?**

Yes. The size of the group does not change how it works, only how many people the unclaimed items are visible to. Clubs and teams tend to use it for subs, kit and who is bringing the gear; streets use it for bins, gritting and shared bookings. Nothing is assigned, everything is claimed.

**What stops this from becoming nagging?**

Two rules that are not settings. It never asks for something that has already happened, and it never asks a person who has nothing left to do. Because they are not settings, nobody can configure them wrong, which is why a group keeps the thread alive instead of muting it.

**How does the group find out it is finished?**

Nexy says it, in the group, once. A thread holds exactly one agreement, so there is a real moment where that agreement is met, and announcing it is what stops people checking in with each other to ask whether it got done.
